name: Nasal strips for sleep

card.summary: Adhesive strips worn across the nose overnight to hold the nostrils open, so breathing through the nose is easier and sleep can be quieter and less disrupted.
card.aka: Breathe Right strips, external nasal dilators
card.note: Adhesive can irritate skin; studies show better nasal airflow but no change in sleep apnea severity measures.

quick.overview:
Nasal strips are small adhesive bandages with a flexible plastic spring inside. Stuck across the bridge and sides of the nose, they gently pull the walls of the nostrils outward. People wear them at night to keep the nose open, with the aim of breathing through the nose while asleep, snoring less and waking more rested.

In appearance-focused communities the payoff is framed as a chain: easier nasal breathing leads to better sleep, which is linked by users to a fresher face, less puffiness and less dry mouth, and it supports nasal-breathing habits that some forum members tie to facial development. Controlled studies have repeatedly measured improved nasal airflow with the strips; results for snoring vary between people.
quick.how: A strip is pressed onto clean, dry skin over the lower part of the nose before bed and peeled off in the morning. Many users pair it with other nasal-breathing practices such as saline rinses or mouth taping. Effects on airflow are felt immediately, so users judge them the first night.
quick.risks: The most commonly reported issue is skin irritation or redness from the adhesive. Reviews find that the strips improve nasal airflow but have not changed measured sleep apnea severity, so they are not a treatment for sleep apnea. People with persistent obstruction or heavy snoring are generally advised by clinicians to have it evaluated.

lead: Nasal strips for sleep are external nasal dilators, best known under the Breathe Right brand, worn across the nose overnight. A strip is an adhesive band with an elastic plastic spine; as the spine tries to flatten, it lifts the sides of the nose and widens the nasal valve, the narrowest part of the airway [1][9]. They were first popularised among athletes and were later marketed for congestion and snoring.

People use them to look and feel better through a chain: a more open nose supports nasal breathing during sleep, which users link to less snoring, fewer wake-ups and a fresher face in the morning. Within looksmaxxing circles they are also discussed alongside mouth taping and myofunctional habits as a low-cost way to encourage nasal breathing.

Research on nasal dilators is extensive. Reviews report that the devices dilate the nasal valve, reduce nasal resistance and improve airflow, with large variation between individuals [1]. A systematic review and meta-analysis found no significant change in apnea-hypopnea index or snoring index in people with obstructive sleep apnea, although nasal breathing itself improved [2]. A 2026 scoping review described the devices as an accessible way of relieving nasal obstruction, with internal dilators showing greater relief than external strips [3].

chain: Nasal airflow improves during the night
Easier nose breathing and quieter, more continuous sleep
More rested look in the morning
angle.text: The strip widens the nasal valve while worn, which makes breathing through the nose easier during sleep. Users connect better sleep and nasal breathing with a more rested appearance and less dry mouth; the strip itself does not change the shape of the nose.

infobox: Across the lower nose, typically overnight or during exercise
Internal dilators such as Nozovent, saline rinses, medical evaluation of obstruction

paras: A nasal strip is a thin adhesive bandage with embedded plastic ribs or splints. It is applied over the bridge and sides of the nose and keeps the sides from collapsing inward during inhalation [9]. During breathing in, negative pressure tends to narrow the nasal valve; the strip stabilises it, and reviews note that airflow improves most on inspiration [1].

Strips come in different sizes and strengths and in clear or skin-toned versions. A separate category, internal dilators such as Nozovent, sits inside the nostrils; reviews often study the two types together [1][2].

In appearance communities the strips appear mainly in nasal-breathing routines. Users describe wearing them to sleep with the mouth closed, sometimes with mouth tape, with the aim of waking with less dry mouth and fewer signs of poor sleep such as puffiness or tired eyes. Some members also connect habitual nasal breathing with jaw and midface development, a claim discussed in separate entries on nasal breathing and mewing.
Others use them for exercise or for temporary relief of a blocked nose, for example during a cold, which is consistent with the way they are marketed.

The device lifts the lateral nasal walls. Studies in healthy volunteers report reduced congestive symptoms and increased airflow through the front of the nose [7][9]. Researchers also use the strips diagnostically: surgeons have applied them in assessments to see whether nasal valve obstruction contributes to a patient's breathing difficulty.

Randomised and crossover studies have examined external dilators in snorers, people with chronic rhinitis, patients with sleep-disordered breathing and healthy people. In a randomised placebo-controlled study of twelve non-obese chronic rhinitis patients, polysomnography was used to assess the effect on snoring [5]. A crossover study of eighteen heavy snorers evaluated effects on nasal airway dimensions, sleep architecture and snoring [6]. A study of 26 patients with sleep-disordered breathing measured respiratory disturbance index with and without the strips [8]. Two randomised controlled trials, published in 2019, examined sleep quality and congestion with Breathe Right strips [4].

A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of fourteen studies found nasal dilators improved nasal breathing but produced no significant change in apnea-hypopnea index, lowest oxygen saturation or snoring index in patients with obstructive sleep apnea; internal dilators showed a small reduction in apnea index [2]. A 2006 review concluded the response varies greatly between individuals and that the strips can reduce snoring in selected patients [1]. In children, an external stent increased nasal inspiratory flow in a randomised study [10]. A study of exercise found that the strips delay the switch to mouth breathing, with small effects on performance [1].

The most commonly mentioned problem is skin irritation from the adhesive [9]. Clinicians note that heavy snoring or persistent obstruction can have causes such as sleep apnea or a deviated septum that a strip does not address, and reviews emphasise the strips have not shown improvement in sleep apnea outcomes [2][3]. Nasal strips are also used by pregnant patients with rhinitis as a drug-free option for subjective relief [11].

timeline.event: Breathe Right strips, made by CNS Inc., are marketed and studied for snoring and exercise; a first wave of trials is published in the late 1990s [8].
A Rhinology review summarises evidence on mechanical nasal dilators [1].
Meta-analysis finds no significant change in sleep apnea measures with nasal dilators [2].
A scoping review reports relief of nasal obstruction, greater with internal devices [3].

lore.intro: Strips are mentioned in nasal-breathing and sleep routines in appearance forums, usually as a gentle starting point before mouth taping.

claims.claim: Wearing strips lets you breathe through your nose all night and wake up looking less puffy and tired
claims.believers: Users say better nasal airflow reduces mouth breathing and dry mouth and improves how rested they look.
claims.experts: Studies show improved nasal airflow with strips; effects on sleep apnea measures were not significant in a meta-analysis [1][2].

claims.claim: Strips help train nasal breathing that supports facial development
claims.believers: Proponents of nasal-breathing approaches say habitual nose breathing influences facial growth.
claims.experts: No published study has tested whether wearing nasal strips changes facial structure.
